title: Animals in Translation: Chapter 1 'My Story'
author: Temple Grandin and Catherine Johnson
source: Animals in Translation: Using the Mysteries of Autism to Decode Animal Behavior (2005)
citation: Grandin, Temple, and Catherine Johnson. Animals in Translation: Using the Mysteries of Autism to Decode Animal Behavior. Scribner, 2005, pp. 1–4.

sections.heading: Chapter 1: My Story

epigraph.quote: Animals don't think in language; they think in pictures, smells, and sounds.

paragraphs: I was born in 1947, and when I was about two and a half years old, I had no speech. I communicated by screaming, peeping, and humming. The doctors told my mother that I was brain-damaged and recommended that I be placed in an institution. My mother refused. Instead, she hired a nanny who played structured turn-taking speech games with me for hours every day.

People with autism have a different nervous system from other people. We are visual thinkers. I think in pictures. Words are like a second language to me. I translate both spoken and written words into full-color movies, complete with sound, which run like a VCR tape in my head. When somebody says a word to me, like 'dog,' I don't see a generalized concept of a dog. I see specific dogs I have known throughout my life: a golden retriever named Rusty, a wirehaired terrier, a German shepherd.

Because of my autism, I feel a natural kinship with animals. Animals don't think in language; they think in pictures, smells, and sounds. They perceive sensory details that normal human beings filter out. Where a human walker sees a peaceful pasture, a cow or a horse notices a flapping piece of plastic, a shadow on the dirt, or a sudden glint of sunlight on a metal gate.

For years, scientists believed that animals didn't have feelings or thoughts, that they were simply stimulus-response machines. But my life with autism taught me that animals have rich emotional and perceptual worlds. To understand animals, humans must learn to translate their sensory reality—to see what they see, feel what they feel, and respect their perceptual intelligence.

My work in designing humane livestock handling facilities around the world came directly from this insight. By getting down on my hands and knees in the chutes and looking through a cow's perspective, I could see the exact shadows, reflections, and drafts that caused them terror. When you fix the environment to respect an animal's sensory perception, fear vanishes and cooperation follows.
